stem: What does MID stand for in MID Server?
rationale: MID = Management, Instrumentation, and Discovery. It's the on-premises agent that bridges the ServiceNow cloud instance and the customer's internal network, executing discovery, integrations, and orchestration on the instance's behalf.

distractor_notes.A: The first word is Management, not Monitoring.
distractor_notes.C: It's Instrumentation, not Integration, and Management, not Monitoring.
distractor_notes.D: The middle word is Instrumentation, not Integration.

stem: What is a MID Server, architecturally?

options.text: A Java application that runs on the customer network and connects out to the ServiceNow instance
A hardware appliance shipped by ServiceNow
A single JAR file with no runtime

rationale: The MID Server is a Java application installed on a host inside the customer's network. It runs the MID software (delivered as JARs) and opens outbound connections to the instance — it isn't an OS, a bare file, or a physical appliance.

distractor_notes.B: It's software you install, not a hardware appliance.
distractor_notes.C: It runs on an OS; it isn't one.
distractor_notes.D: A JAR is just packaging; the MID Server is the running Java process.

stem: How many ServiceNow instances can a single MID Server connect to?
rationale: A MID Server record holds one instance URL and one credential set, so it connects to exactly one instance. To serve a second instance you install another MID Server with its own configuration.

distractor_notes.A: It can't target multiple instances from one record.
distractor_notes.B: Ten is arbitrary and not how the MID Server works.
distractor_notes.D: There's no 255 limit; the design ties one MID Server to one instance.

stem: How does a MID Server communicate with the ServiceNow instance?

options.text: It responds to inbound connections over HTTPS
It initiates outbound connections over HTTP
It responds to inbound connections over HTTP
It initiates outbound connections over HTTPS

rationale: The MID Server always initiates the connection outbound over HTTPS — it polls the instance for work and posts results. Because it's outbound-only and encrypted, no inbound firewall holes to the MID Server are required, which is a key security advantage.

distractor_notes.A: It initiates, it doesn't wait for inbound connections.
distractor_notes.B: Production instances use HTTPS, not HTTP.
distractor_notes.C: Communication is HTTPS, not plain HTTP, and outbound-initiated.

stem: Which outbound port must be open from the customer network so the MID Server can reach a ServiceNow cloud instance?
rationale: Cloud instances are reached over TLS on TCP 443, and the MID Server connects outbound. Opening only outbound 443 to *.service-now.com is enough — and avoids exposing unnecessary services.

distractor_notes.A: 636 is LDAPS, used for directory services, not instance communication.
distractor_notes.B: Plain HTTP (80) is disabled for production instances in favor of TLS.
distractor_notes.C: 8080 is sometimes used by on-prem appliances, not the public cloud instance.

stem: When is the MID Server config.xml read and applied?

options.text: Each time the file is saved
When the MID Server application starts

rationale: config.xml is loaded at MID Server startup, so any edits to it take effect only after you restart the MID Server service. Saving the file alone doesn't apply the change to the running process.

distractor_notes.A: Saving persists the file but doesn't reload it into the running MID Server.
distractor_notes.B: Stopping the service doesn't apply config; the next start does.
distractor_notes.C: Config is read on startup regardless of upgrades.

stem: By default, how often does a MID Server check for upgrades?
rationale: The MID Server polls for an available upgrade every 30 minutes by default — a balance between picking up patches promptly and not hammering the upgrade service. Don't confuse this with the 5-minute Service Mapping heartbeat.

distractor_notes.A: 15 minutes isn't the documented default.
distractor_notes.B: 5 minutes is the Service Mapping heartbeat interval, not the upgrade check.
distractor_notes.C: 60 minutes is slower than the default.

stem: What is the correct order of the four ServiceNow Discovery phases?
rationale: Horizontal Discovery runs Port Scan (Shazzam finds open ports), then Classification (decides what kind of device it is and which probes/patterns to use), then Identification (creates/updates the CI), then Exploration (gathers detailed attributes and relationships).

distractor_notes.B: You must scan ports before you can classify what's responding.
distractor_notes.C: Identification can't precede the port scan and classification that feed it.
distractor_notes.D: This is the reverse of the actual order.

stem: Which Discovery phase uses the Shazzam probe?
rationale: Shazzam is the port-scanning probe that opens the Port Scan phase — it pings the target range and reports which ports respond. Those open-port results drive classification, telling Discovery what kind of device it's likely dealing with.

distractor_notes.A: Classification consumes Shazzam's results; it isn't the Shazzam phase.
distractor_notes.C: Exploration gathers deep attributes later in the process.
distractor_notes.D: Identification creates/updates the CI after classification.

stem: On what basis does ServiceNow Discovery primarily classify computers?
rationale: Discovery classifies a computer by its operating system — Windows, Linux, Unix — which determines the class (e.g., Windows Server) and which probes/patterns run next. Other facts like CPU or name are collected later but don't drive the initial classification.

distractor_notes.A: WMI is a collection protocol, not the classification criterion.
distractor_notes.C: CPU type is inventory detail, not the classification key.
distractor_notes.D: NetBIOS name aids targeting/de-duplication, not classification.

stem: In which phase(s) is a server's RAM value typically discovered?
rationale: Detailed hardware attributes like RAM are gathered in the later phases — identification confirms the CI and exploration collects rich attributes. The early phases (port scan, classification) only determine reachability and device type.

distractor_notes.A: Classification decides device type, not detailed attributes like RAM.
distractor_notes.C: Port scan only finds open ports; it reads no hardware detail.
distractor_notes.D: Neither of these early phases collects RAM.

stem: Which Discovery phase is responsible for mapping application-to-host relationships?
rationale: Exploration runs the pattern logic that correlates discovered applications with their hosting infrastructure, producing the application-to-host relationships. The earlier phases only find ports, decide device type, and create the base CI.

distractor_notes.A: Identification creates/updates the CI but defers deep relationship discovery to exploration.
distractor_notes.C: Classification selects probes/patterns; it doesn't build relationships.
distractor_notes.D: Port scan only enumerates open ports.

stem: Which component typically queries target hosts to gather discovery data?
rationale: Probes are the active collectors — they reach out to targets over SSH, WMI, SNMP, etc., and bring data back. Sensors then parse those results, and classifiers decide what kind of device it is; the probe is the part that actually queries the host.

distractor_notes.A: Classifiers categorize based on results; they don't reach out to targets.
distractor_notes.B: Sensors process the data probes return; they don't query the host.
distractor_notes.C: Business rules run on instance records, not against discovery targets.

stem: ServiceNow Discovery performs which type of discovery?
rationale: Discovery is horizontal: it sweeps infrastructure (servers, network, storage, apps) and populates CIs and their relationships broadly. Service Mapping, by contrast, is top-down — it starts from a service and drills into its dependencies.

distractor_notes.A: Top-down is Service Mapping's approach, not horizontal Discovery.
distractor_notes.B: 'Up-down' isn't a recognized discovery type.
distractor_notes.C: 'Vertical discovery' isn't ServiceNow's term for the Discovery engine.

stem: Approximately how many host IPs are in the network 180.181.0.0/16 that a Discovery schedule would scan?
rationale: A /16 leaves 32-16 = 16 host bits, so 2^16 = 65,536 addresses. That's the size of the range Discovery would port-scan unless exclusions are defined — useful for estimating scan scope and MID Server load.

distractor_notes.B: ~1 million would be roughly a /12.
distractor_notes.C: ~16 million (2^24) is a /8, far larger than a /16.
distractor_notes.D: 256 is a /24 (8 host bits), not a /16.

stem: Which of the following is a public IP address?
rationale: 203.0.113.0/24 is outside the RFC1918 private ranges, so it's a public address. The others are private: 10.0.0.0/8, 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255, and 192.168.0.0/16 are all reserved for internal networks.

distractor_notes.B: 172.20.5.9 is in the private 172.16.0.0/12 range.
distractor_notes.C: 10.0.6.8 is in the private 10.0.0.0/8 range.

stem: A domain user with local admin can discover most Windows hosts, but which target needs higher-level (domain) credentials for full discovery?
rationale: Domain Controllers run core directory services (AD, and often DNS/DHCP) that local admin can't fully read. Properly classifying and exploring a DC needs elevated, domain-level credentials, unlike ordinary member servers.

distractor_notes.A: A print server doesn't require domain-level rights for discovery.
distractor_notes.B: A workstation is discoverable with the standard local-admin account.
distractor_notes.D: A standalone file server is fine with local admin.

stem: A Service Mapping discovery returns 'Failed to access target system. Access is denied.' on a Windows host. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: A CLI permissions error on Unix

rationale: 'Access is denied' on Windows almost always means the credential the MID Server used isn't valid for that host or lacks the local-admin rights WMI needs. The fix is correcting the credential or its privileges, not chasing SSO or reconciliation.

distractor_notes.A: CLI/Unix permissions are a different platform and error path.
distractor_notes.B: SSO governs interactive logins, not the MID Server's WMI authentication.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation conflicts are CMDB data issues, not access-denied at the host.

stem: With three MID Servers in a load-balanced cluster but Shazzam cluster support disabled, how is work distributed?

options.text: One MID Server runs the port scan
Only one MID Server is used for every phase
All three run the port scan; one does classification
All three run every phase simultaneously

rationale: Without Shazzam cluster support, the port scan isn't distributed — a single MID Server handles it. Once responsive IPs are known, the later classification and exploration work is load-balanced across all three MID Servers.

distractor_notes.B: The later phases do use all three; it isn't one MID for everything.
distractor_notes.C: The port scan is the part that's NOT distributed here; only one MID does it.
distractor_notes.D: The port scan stays on a single MID without Shazzam clustering.

stem: Which Discovery phase decides whether a device should be created or updated in the CMDB?
rationale: Identification matches the gathered data against the CI's identifier rules and decides: update an existing CI or insert a new one. Port scan and classification prepare the way, and exploration enriches the record after identity is settled.

distractor_notes.A: Port scan finds open ports; it makes no create/update decision.
distractor_notes.B: Exploration adds attributes after the CI already exists.
distractor_notes.C: Classification picks probes/patterns based on device type, not CI identity.

stem: In probe-and-sensor discovery, what is the sensor's role?

options.text: To open ports on the target
To parse the data a probe returns and update the CMDB accordingly
To query the target host directly

rationale: Probes collect; sensors interpret. The sensor takes the probe's returned payload, parses it, and writes the resulting CI data and relationships to the CMDB. It's the processing half of the probe-and-sensor pair.

distractor_notes.A: Sensors don't scan ports; Shazzam does that.
distractor_notes.B: Credentials live in Credential Management, not in sensors.
distractor_notes.D: Querying the host is the probe's job, not the sensor's.

stem: What does a Discovery classifier do?

options.text: Stores the XML payload returned from the MID Server
Evaluates initial scan results to determine the device type and which probes/patterns to run next

rationale: Classifiers look at the early evidence (open ports, banners, basic responses) and decide what the target is — Windows, Linux, a network device — then route to the right probes or patterns. They categorize; they don't collect or reconcile.

distractor_notes.A: Payloads sit in the ECC Queue, not in classifiers.
distractor_notes.B: Reconciliation is an IRE function, unrelated to classification.
distractor_notes.D: Reaching out over SSH is a probe action, not a classifier's.

stem: In the ECC Queue, what does an 'Output' record represent?

options.text: Work sent from the instance out to the MID Server
A result returning from the MID Server to the instance

rationale: Direction is from the instance's point of view: Output flows out to the MID Server (the probe/command to run), and Input comes back in (the result). So an Output record is the instruction the MID Server picks up and executes.

distractor_notes.A: Reconciliation happens in IRE, not as an ECC record type.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials aren't stored in the ECC Queue.
distractor_notes.D: A returning result is an Input record, not Output.

stem: What is the MID Server's role relative to the instance and the internal network?

options.text: A conduit that runs probes/commands on the internal network on the instance's behalf and returns results
A monitoring tool that generates alerts

rationale: The MID Server sits between the cloud instance and the on-prem network, executing the work the instance can't reach directly — discovery probes, pattern commands, integrations — and posting results back. It's the bridge, not a data store or a monitoring product.

distractor_notes.B: The CMDB stores CIs; the MID Server gathers data to populate it.
distractor_notes.C: It's a software conduit, not a firewall.
distractor_notes.D: Alerts come from Event Management/monitoring, not the MID Server itself.

stem: Service Mapping reports: 'Failed to identify CI on host myHostName. The application port 1433 is closed.' What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The Discovery pattern isn't configured to collect the port
The application process isn't running/listening on that port

rationale: A closed port means nothing is listening there — the database/application process is down or not bound to 1433 — so the engine can't reach it to identify the CI. You verify and start the process (or correct the expected port) before retrying.

distractor_notes.A: Entry points define where mapping starts; they don't make a listening port open or closed.
distractor_notes.B: A rule misconfig would surface differently; here the port itself is closed.
distractor_notes.C: The error fires because the port can't be reached at all, before pattern collection matters.

stem: Which set of protocols does Service Mapping commonly use to discover target CIs?
rationale: WMI reaches Windows hosts, SSH reaches Unix/Linux and many network devices, and SNMP polls network gear. Together they cover the bulk of CI types Service Mapping discovers. SMTP/LDAP/HTTP serve other functions and aren't the core discovery protocol set.

distractor_notes.A: SMTP/FTP aren't the discovery protocols.
distractor_notes.B: LDAP locates directory objects but doesn't gather host configuration detail.
distractor_notes.C: SMTP is for email; it isn't a discovery protocol.

stem: Why does the MID Server's outbound-only design improve security posture?

options.text: No inbound firewall rules to the MID Server are required
It encrypts the CMDB at rest
It eliminates the need for credentials

rationale: Because the MID Server initiates everything outbound to the instance, you never have to open inbound ports to it from the internet. That shrinks the attack surface — there's no listening service for an outside attacker to target.

distractor_notes.B: CMDB encryption is a separate platform concern, not a MID Server function.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials are still required to authenticate to targets.
distractor_notes.D: It permits the outbound traffic it needs (443); it doesn't block all outbound.

stem: What does a Discovery Schedule define?

options.text: What to discover (IP ranges/targets), when, and with which MID Server

rationale: A Discovery Schedule ties together the scope (IP ranges or targets), the timing (when it runs), and the MID Server(s) that execute it. It's the orchestration record that drives horizontal discovery runs.

distractor_notes.B: Credentials are managed separately in Credential Management.
distractor_notes.C: Health thresholds belong to CMDB Health, not discovery schedules.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation precedence is an IRE setting, unrelated to schedules.

stem: How does pattern-based discovery differ from classic probe-and-sensor discovery?

options.text: Patterns use a declarative, step-based language
Patterns store data outside the CMDB
Patterns run on the instance without a MID Server

rationale: Patterns express discovery as ordered, declarative steps you build in Pattern Designer, which is easier to maintain and extend than hand-coded probe/sensor scripts. Both still run via the MID Server, use credentials, and write to the CMDB.

distractor_notes.B: Both approaches populate the CMDB.
distractor_notes.C: Patterns still execute through the MID Server against targets.
distractor_notes.D: Credentials are required either way to reach hosts.

stem: How can you control which MID Server is used for a given discovery target?

options.text: Edit the target host's hosts file
Assign capabilities, applications, and IP ranges to the MID Server so it's selected for matching work

rationale: MID Server selection is driven by its configured capabilities, applications, and IP-range scope. Discovery picks the MID Server whose configuration matches the work, so you steer traffic by configuring those attributes rather than by hacks.

distractor_notes.A: A host's hosts file doesn't determine MID Server selection.
distractor_notes.B: Health thresholds are unrelated to MID Server routing.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting MID Servers reduces capacity; capabilities/IP scoping is the right control.

stem: You need to see the raw probe payloads exchanged with the MID Server for a discovery. Where do you look?
rationale: The ECC Queue holds the actual payloads sent to and returned from the MID Server. When you need the literal probe input/output (XML), the ECC Queue is the place — whereas the Discovery Log shows the higher-level step-by-step narrative.

distractor_notes.B: The service catalog is for request items, unrelated to discovery payloads.
distractor_notes.C: Health shows data-quality scores, not probe payloads.
distractor_notes.D: The email log tracks notifications.

stem: Approximately how many addresses are in a /24 network that Discovery would scan?
rationale: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, so 2^8 = 256 addresses. It's the common 'class C' subnet size and a handy unit when scoping Discovery schedules and estimating scan time.

distractor_notes.A: 1,024 would be a /22.
distractor_notes.B: 16 would be a /28.

stem: Discovery is slow and the MID Server host is resource-constrained. What is the most appropriate scaling response?

options.text: Add MID Servers (and/or memory) and load-balance the work across a cluster
Delete discovered CIs to reduce load
Disable IRE to speed things up
Open inbound port 443 to the MID Server

rationale: MID Server throughput scales horizontally: add MID Servers (or memory) and put them in a load-balanced cluster so phases like classification and exploration spread across them. That relieves a single constrained host without compromising data integrity.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting CIs destroys data and doesn't address MID Server capacity.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling IRE would corrupt the CMDB, not safely speed discovery.
distractor_notes.D: Inbound 443 isn't needed (MID Server is outbound-only) and doesn't add capacity.

stem: When Service Mapping reaches a host during top-down discovery, how is the host's detailed inventory gathered?

options.text: It asks the user to enter the details manually
It copies details from a similar host
It reads the host details from the service map cache only

rationale: Top-down mapping leans on horizontal discovery for host depth: when it hits a host, it runs the standard host discovery (via the MID Server) to populate OS, hardware, and software, then IRE matches/updates the CI. Service Mapping focuses on the service topology; host detail comes from discovery.

distractor_notes.A: Host details are discovered, not hand-entered.
distractor_notes.B: Details are gathered from the host itself, not copied from another.
distractor_notes.C: There's no cache substitute for actually discovering the host.

stem: What feeds the Classification phase its inputs?

options.text: The open ports and responses found during the Port Scan

rationale: Classification reasons over what the port scan found — which ports answered and how — to decide the device type and which probes/patterns to launch. Without the Shazzam results, it has nothing to classify on.

distractor_notes.A: Notification logs are unrelated to discovery classification.
distractor_notes.C: Health scores are computed later and don't drive classification.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation precedence governs attribute authority, not classification input.

stem: How does the instance know a MID Server is alive and reachable?

options.text: The MID Server regularly posts a heartbeat/status to the instance
The instance SSHes into the MID Server host
The MID Server emails a status report

rationale: The MID Server sends a periodic heartbeat/status check-in to the instance. If those stop arriving, the instance marks the MID Server Down — which is the first thing to verify when discoveries silently stop running.

distractor_notes.B: The instance never connects inbound to the MID Server; the MID Server checks in outbound.
distractor_notes.C: Status is reported via the heartbeat mechanism, not email.
distractor_notes.D: CMDB Health measures data quality, not MID Server liveness.

stem: Which tool gives the step-by-step narrative of which patterns, sections, and steps ran during a Service Mapping discovery?
rationale: The Discovery Log is the human-readable trace of a mapping run, expanding pattern → section → step with success/failure at each node. The ECC Queue, by contrast, holds the raw payloads; you use the log to follow the logic and the queue to inspect the data.

distractor_notes.B: The ECC Queue shows payloads, not the section/step narrative.
distractor_notes.C: The slow query log is about database queries, unrelated to discovery.
distractor_notes.D: The transaction log tracks instance request performance, not discovery steps.

stem: What is the goal of the Exploration phase?

options.text: To gather detailed attributes and relationships for an already-identified CI
To create the CI record for the first time
To find which ports are open

rationale: By exploration, the CI already exists; this phase enriches it — deep attributes, installed software, and the relationships (like application-to-host) that give the CMDB its dependency value. The earlier phases scanned, classified, and identified.

distractor_notes.B: Creating the CI is identification; exploration enriches it afterward.
distractor_notes.C: Deciding device type is classification.
distractor_notes.D: Finding open ports is the port scan's job.

stem: A target subnet is only reachable from one network zone. How do you ensure the correct MID Server handles it?

options.text: Scope that MID Server to the subnet's IP range so it's selected for those targets
Give every MID Server every credential
Disable the other MID Servers permanently

rationale: Assign the in-zone MID Server an IP-range that covers the subnet so discovery routes that work to it — the only MID Server that can actually reach those hosts. IP-range scoping is the supported way to match work to network reachability.

distractor_notes.B: Credentials don't fix network reachability; the wrong-zone MID Server still can't connect.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling others reduces capacity globally; scoping is the targeted fix.
distractor_notes.D: Heartbeat frequency doesn't influence target routing.

stem: Which statement about MID Server applications is correct?

options.text: One MID Server can support multiple ITOM applications
Each application requires its own dedicated MID Server with no overlap
MID Servers cannot run Service Mapping
A MID Server can only ever run Discovery

rationale: A single MID Server can be enabled for several applications at once — Discovery, Service Mapping, Orchestration, Event Management — controlled by its capabilities/applications configuration. You scale out for capacity, not because each app needs its own MID Server.

distractor_notes.B: Dedicated MID Servers per app aren't required, though you may separate by load/zone.
distractor_notes.C: Service Mapping specifically relies on the MID Server.
distractor_notes.D: It supports more than Discovery; Service Mapping and others run on it too.

stem: What is the key difference between horizontal Discovery and Service Mapping?

options.text: Service Mapping does not use the CMDB
Discovery is top-down; Service Mapping is horizontal

rationale: Discovery sweeps the estate to populate CIs and basic relationships (horizontal). Service Mapping starts from a business service's entry point and follows the dependency chain (top-down) to build a precise service map. They complement each other and both write to the CMDB.

distractor_notes.A: Service Mapping populates and reads the CMDB just like Discovery.
distractor_notes.B: They have different scopes and directions.
distractor_notes.D: It's the reverse — Discovery is horizontal, Service Mapping is top-down.

stem: All discoveries on one zone suddenly stop and tasks aren't being picked up. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the responsible MID Server is Up

rationale: If a MID Server is Down or unvalidated, its ECC Queue output tasks sit unprocessed and discoveries appear to stall. Confirming the MID Server's heartbeat/status (and that it's validated and reachable) is the first triage step.

distractor_notes.A: A low health score doesn't stop discoveries from running.
distractor_notes.B: Catalog items are unrelated to discovery execution.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation ordering affects attribute writes, not whether tasks are picked up.

stem: Before a newly installed MID Server can be used, what must happen?

options.text: It must be added to the service catalog
Inbound port 443 must be opened to it
It must be validated (its certificate/connection approved) on the instance

rationale: A new MID Server connects and then must be validated on the instance before it will process work — this confirms its identity/certificate and authorizes it. Until validated, it can't run discoveries.

distractor_notes.A: The service catalog is unrelated to MID Server activation.
distractor_notes.B: The MID Server is outbound-only; no inbound 443 is required.
distractor_notes.C: Credentials are needed to discover targets, not deleted.

stem: An ECC Queue record in the 'Ready' state means what?

options.text: It has already been processed and closed
It is queued and ready to be picked up/processed by its consumer
It encountered an error and was discarded
It is waiting indefinitely and will never run

rationale: 'Ready' means the record is set to be consumed — an Output/Ready task is ready for the MID Server to take, and an Input/Ready result is ready for the instance to process. It's the actionable state in the queue's lifecycle.

distractor_notes.A: Processed records move to Processed, not Ready.
distractor_notes.C: Errors move to an error state, not Ready.
distractor_notes.D: Ready is actively pollable, not a permanent wait.

stem: Discovery reaches a group of Linux hosts but fails to collect data, logging authentication errors. What is the most likely configuration to fix?

options.text: Provide valid SSH credentials accessible to the MID Server's credential store
Open an inbound firewall port on each host
Add a watch list to the hosts

rationale: Linux discovery uses SSH; authentication errors point to missing or invalid SSH credentials. Storing working SSH credentials for the MID Server to use resolves it. The MID Server still connects outbound, so inbound ports aren't the fix.

distractor_notes.B: The MID Server connects outbound to hosts; inbound ports aren't the issue.
distractor_notes.C: Watch lists handle notifications, not authentication.
distractor_notes.D: Health thresholds don't affect host authentication.

stem: Targets live in a network segment that only one MID Server can reach. How do you ensure Discovery uses the right MID Server for those targets?

options.text: Use MID Server selection based on capabilities and IP ranges
Run Discovery without any MID Server

rationale: MID Server selection uses capabilities, IP ranges, and applications so the platform picks a MID Server that can actually reach the targets. That routes the segment's discovery to the correct MID Server without removing others.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting other MID Servers harms coverage elsewhere.
distractor_notes.C: Discovery of remote targets requires a MID Server.
distractor_notes.D: Coalesce matches import records.

stem: At the start of a Discovery run, the platform needs to find which devices are up and which ports are open across an IP range. Which probe performs this port scan?
rationale: Shazzam is the port-scanning probe that detects active devices and open ports across the range during the scanning phase, guiding which classifiers run next.

distractor_notes.B: Transform maps move imported data.
distractor_notes.C: Connection sections are part of Service Mapping patterns, not the initial scan.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation rules manage attribute authority.

stem: Discovery detects a running process on a host but doesn't know what application it is, so it isn't classified. Which mechanism determines the application from the process?
rationale: Process classifiers match running processes (and ports/parameters) to applications, so Discovery can classify and trigger the right pattern to gather details. Without a matching classifier, the app may show as generic.

distractor_notes.B: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.

stem: Discovery is slow because it tries many credentials against each target before finding the one that works. Which feature remembers the successful credential to speed future runs?
rationale: Credential affinity records which credential succeeded for a target so subsequent runs try it first, reducing failed attempts and speeding discovery.

distractor_notes.B: Reconciliation rules govern attribute authority, not credential reuse.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Service groups organize services, not credentials.

stem: You need to troubleshoot the messages exchanged between the instance and a MID Server during Discovery. Where do you look?
rationale: The ECC Queue holds the input/output messages between the instance and MID Servers (probes sent, results returned). It's the go-to place to trace what a MID Server was asked to do and what it returned.

distractor_notes.B: The Service Catalog is for ordering services.
distractor_notes.C: Update set logs track configuration moves.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge bases store articles.

stem: Some Linux discovery commands require elevated privileges, but your account isn't root. How is this typically handled?

options.text: Configure SSH credentials to use sudo for the elevated commands
Share the root password with all users
Disable the commands that need elevation
Run Discovery as a UI policy

rationale: SSH credentials can be configured to use sudo so specific commands run with elevation without logging in as root, following least-privilege practice.

distractor_notes.B: Sharing root credentials is insecure and unnecessary.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling needed commands leaves the CI incomplete.
distractor_notes.D: UI policies don't run discovery commands.

stem: Network devices like routers and switches need to be discovered. Which credential type does Discovery typically use for them?
rationale: Network devices are commonly discovered using SNMP, so SNMP credentials (community strings or SNMPv3) are configured for them. SSH/Windows credentials suit servers, not typical network gear.

distractor_notes.B: SSH is for Unix/Linux hosts, not standard network-device discovery.
distractor_notes.C: Windows credentials are for Windows hosts.
distractor_notes.D: OAuth is for web APIs, not SNMP device discovery.

stem: What does a Discovery schedule primarily define?

options.text: Which IP ranges to discover and when to run
The authoritative source for an attribute

rationale: A Discovery schedule defines the targets (IP ranges) and timing (when/how often) for a Discovery run, along with the MID Server behavior. It's the controller for what gets scanned and when.

distractor_notes.B: Notification recipients are configured on notifications.
distractor_notes.C: Attribute authority is set by reconciliation rules.
distractor_notes.D: Branding is unrelated to Discovery.

stem: In horizontal Discovery, which sequence reflects the general phase order?

options.text: Scanning (Shazzam) to classification to identification to exploration
Exploration to scanning to classification to identification
Identification to scanning to exploration to classification
Classification to exploration to scanning to identification

rationale: Discovery generally goes scanning (find active devices/ports via Shazzam), classification (what kind of device/app), identification (match/create the CI via IRE), then exploration (gather detailed attributes and relationships).

distractor_notes.B: Exploration is last, not first.
distractor_notes.C: Scanning comes first, not identification.
distractor_notes.D: Scanning is the first phase, not third.

stem: Which TWO statements about Discovery credentials are correct?

options.text: Credentials are stored securely and used by the MID Server to access targets
Credential affinity speeds runs by reusing the credential that worked
Credentials must be embedded in every probe by hand
SNMP is used for authenticating to the Service Portal

rationale: Credentials live in a secure store and the MID Server uses them to reach targets, while credential affinity reuses successful credentials to speed discovery. Probes don't embed credentials by hand, and SNMP is for network devices, not portal login.

distractor_notes.C: Credentials are centrally stored, not hand-embedded per probe.
distractor_notes.D: SNMP discovers network devices; it isn't portal authentication.

stem: Which TWO are true of the MID Server in Discovery?

options.text: It initiates outbound connections to the instance
It executes probes/patterns against targets inside the network
It requires inbound ports opened to each target from the cloud

rationale: The MID Server connects outbound to the instance and runs probes/patterns against internal targets — no inbound exposure needed. The CMDB lives on the instance, not the MID Server.

distractor_notes.C: Outbound connections avoid opening inbound ports.
distractor_notes.D: The CMDB is on the instance; the MID Server is a connectivity/execution bridge.
